hero.kicker: AN OPEN STANDARD + A COMMUNITY-OWNED COMMONS
hero.title: One shared format for BASE exit data.
hero.sub: Today every app and database stores exit sites differently, and nothing is compatible — when a platform shuts down, its data disappears with it. With a shared format, any app can read and contribute the same data, and the knowledge outlives the tools.

problem.title: The same number, stored twice, in two units.
problem.body: In a widely-used community dataset, whole field pairs carry the same physical quantity in metres and feet, under names that disclose neither the unit nor the meaning. A consumer that guesses wrong is off by a factor of 3.28 — on a number people use to choose a slider configuration. That is what happens to every schema that grows without a standard.
problem.codeCommentGood: // OpenExit — the unit is in the name

standard.title: The standard
standard.body: A versioned, machine-validated specification for how exit sites are described — location, heights, access, landings, hazards. Free to implement for anyone, even proprietary apps (CC0).

commons.title: The commons
commons.body: A public database of exit sites in that format, contributed by jumpers, reviewed by humans before anything publishes, and free for every app to use (ODbL).

foundation.title: The foundation
foundation.body: An independent non-profit — not a company, not an app — that owns the name and infrastructure for one purpose: keeping the standard and the data open, neutral, and alive.

locks.title: Why the data belongs to the community, forever

lock1.title: Everyone holds a copy
lock1.body: Anyone is free to copy the whole database. Thousands of copies means no one can ever delete it or hold it hostage.

lock2.title: The licence forbids enclosure
lock2.body: You can build on the data, even commercially — but improvements to the database must be shared back. Nobody can take it private.

lock3.title: Contributors keep their rights
lock3.body: You lend your contribution to the commons — you never surrender it. Even the licence can only change by a vote of the contributors themselves.

contribute.title: Know a site? Add it from your phone.
contribute.body: Drop a pin, answer a short set of questions, and a human moderator reviews everything before it publishes. Corrections work the same way — and every contribution keeps your name on it, permanently.
